nameStory: The mayapple gets its name from its apple-like fruit that ripens in May, though the timing can stretch into early summer. Early settlers and Indigenous peoples recognized this plant as a reliable sign of spring's bounty, with its umbrella-like leaves emerging just as the forest floor warms up.
description: Mayapple is a curious woodland perennial that looks like tiny green umbrellas popping up from the forest floor. Each plant sends up one or two large, deeply-lobed leaves that can span 6-12 inches across, held up by sturdy stems reaching 12-18 inches tall. The whole plant has an almost tropical appearance that seems out of place in our New England woods, creating distinctive colonies that spread by underground rhizomes.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, umbrella-like leaves divided into 5-9 deep lobes radiating from where the stem attaches in the center (like spokes of an umbrella). The leaves feel smooth and waxy to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single white flower with 6-9 waxy petals hangs beneath the leaves where two stems fork, blooming in May. The flower has a sweet, almost rose-like fragrance and nods downward like it's hiding.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Yellow-green, egg-shaped berry about 2 inches long ripens in summer, hanging beneath the leaves. When ripe, it smells sweet and tropical, almost like a mix of strawberry and mango.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms colonies of umbrella-like plants, with some having one leaf (non-flowering) and others having two leaves joined at a fork (flowering). The stems are thick, smooth, and pale green.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves emerge in spring as tightly furled umbrellas that slowly unfold, and by summer they create dense patches that can carpet the forest floor in shade.

habitat: Mayapples thrive in rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly favoring areas with deep, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Look for them in partial to deep shade under maples, oaks, and beech trees, often on gentle slopes or in forest clearings. They commonly grow alongside trilliums, wild ginger, and bloodroot in these nutrient-rich woodland communities.

seasonality.spring: Distinctive furled leaves push through the soil in April, slowly unfurling like opening umbrellas. White flowers appear in May beneath the leaves, filling the air with their sweet fragrance.
seasonality.summer: Leaves reach full size creating umbrella-like canopies, and yellow-green fruits ripen by midsummer. The colony is at its most impressive, forming dense patches of tropical-looking foliage.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow and begin to wither, with fruits either eaten by wildlife or fallen. The above-ground parts die back completely as the plant prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground presence, existing only as underground rhizomes. Look for last year's dried stems as clues to where colonies will emerge next spring.

funFact: Mayapple is like a botanical pharmacy - its roots contain podophyllin, a compound that has been used to treat certain types of cancer and genital warts, making this humble woodland plant a source of modern medicine hiding in plain sight.
confusionNotes: Young mayapples might be confused with emerging trilliums, but remember that mayapples have umbrella leaves attached in the center while trillium leaves whorl around the stem in threes. The memory trick: mayapples hold umbrellas, trilliums count to three.
contextualKnowledge: While the ripe fruit is edible and was used by Indigenous peoples, all other parts of the mayapple plant are toxic, containing compounds that can cause serious illness. The plant's scientific name Podophyllum literally means "duck foot," referring to the webbed appearance of the lobed leaves.
compareHints: Mayapple is the only member of its genus in North America, making it fairly unique in our region. Within the barberry family, it's most easily distinguished from other relatives like barberry shrubs by its herbaceous nature and distinctive umbrella-shaped leaves. No other New England plant has quite the same combination of large, centrally-attached lobed leaves and single drooping white flowers.
